 529 Plans Aren’t Just for Kids. Grandparents Are Using Them as a Tax Shelter
 The tax code rewards grandparents who give college money early and quietly lets them keep control of every dollar they hand over. Here is the move that estate planners use to move six figures out of a taxable estate without…
 By Vilma Rios 
 Published October 24, 2026, 5:00am ET · 4 min read 
 Tax Master desk. Editor: Vilma Rios .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 A grandparent can deposit $95,000 per grandchild in 2026, or $190,000 as a couple, without triggering gift tax using the five-year superfunding election.
 A couple superfunding three grandchildren moves $570,000 out of their taxable estate, shielding roughly $408,000 in federal estate taxes at the 40% rate.
 Grandparents stay in control as account owners, can switch beneficiaries to another family member tax-free, and can reclaim contributions without income tax if plans change.

 Many grandparents are exploring strategies like 529 plans to provide for their grandchildren's education, offering both future security and tax benefits. © imtmphoto / iStock via Getty Images 
 Most grandparents who help with college write a check when the tuition bill shows up. The tax code quietly rewards the ones who write a much bigger check years earlier, into a 529 plan, and keep the strings attached.
 A provision in Section 529 of the Internal Revenue Code lets a grandparent load five years of tax-free gifts into a grandchild’s account at once. That money leaves the taxable estate right away and grows tax-free. It also stays under the grandparent’s control: they can change the beneficiary or even take the money back. Few other gifts let you give money away and keep the steering wheel.
 Five-Year Election Turns $19,000 Into $95,000
 For tax year 2026, the annual gift-tax exclusion remains at $19,000 per recipient. Give more than that to one person in a year and the excess starts using up your lifetime exemption.
 Section 529(c)(2)(B) carves out an exception. When 529 contributions top the annual limit, the donor can choose to spread them “ratably over the 5-year period beginning with such calendar year”. Planners call this super-funding . In 2026, one grandparent can put in $95,000 per grandchild without using the lifetime exemption, and a married couple can put in $190,000.
 You make the election on the gift tax return, Form 709. There’s one catch: during those five years, any other gift to that grandchild counts against your lifetime exemption.
 Worked Example: $570,000 Leaves a Taxable Estate
 Picture a composite couple in their early 70s. They have three grandchildren and an estate well above the federal exemption. In 2026, each spouse makes the five-year election for each grandchild. This example assumes 6% annual growth and puts every dollar in the top estate-tax bracket.
 Step 
 Amount 
 One spouse, one grandchild 
 $95,000 
 Both spouses, one grandchild 
 $190,000 
 Both spouses, three grandchildren 
 $570,000 
 Value after 10 years at 6% 
 $1,020,783 
 Federal estate tax avoided at 40% 
 $408,313 
 Section 529(c)(4)(A) says no amount “shall be includible in the gross estate of any individual” because of an interest in a 529. That protection covers the growth too. Estate amounts over $1,000,000 are taxed at 40%, so about $408,000 stays with the family.
 Grandparents Keep Control of the Money
 Grandparents can be the account owner, so the grandchild never owns the money outright. If one grandchild skips college, the owner can switch the account to a sibling or cousin. Moving it to a “member of the family of the old beneficiary” doesn’t count as a taxable distribution.
 If the owner needs the money back, contributions come out tax-free because they’re a return of the investment. Earnings face income tax plus an additional 10% tax. That’s the shelter: the money sits outside the estate but stays within reach.
 Leftover money has another exit. A beneficiary can roll up to $35,000 over their lifetime into a Roth IRA if the account has been open more than 15 years. Each year’s rollover is capped at the Roth contribution limit.
 Dying Within Five Years Pulls Money Back In
 Super-funding comes with a catch. Under Section 529(c)(4)(C), if a donor who made the election dies before the five years are up, the share “properly allocable to periods after the date of death” goes back into the gross estate. The earlier you super-fund, the sooner the full gift counts.
 Who Actually Benefits, Even Without an Estate Tax Bill
 The federal estate exclusion is $15,000,000 for people who die in 2026. Very few families owe the tax: of returns filed in 2024, only 2,663 owed any net estate tax. Still, older households hold most of the money. Households headed by people 70 and older control 33.6% of U.S. household net worth.
 For most of these families, the benefit is tax-free growth plus more flexibility. Starting in 2026, a 529 can pay up to $20,000 a year per student for K-12 costs. Under the simplified FAFSA , distributions from a grandparent-owned 529 no longer count as student income. Many states also offer a state income tax deduction for contributions, and the rules differ widely from state to state.
 Moves to Make Before December 31
 Fund by year-end. Contributions made by December 31 count toward 2026 and start the five-year period.
 File the election. Choose five-year averaging on Form 709 by the gift-tax deadline, which is generally April 15, 2027.
 Name a replacement owner. The account stays out of your estate either way, but naming a replacement keeps a person you trust in control of it.
 The most common mistake is super-funding and then forgetting the election. Without the five-year averaging election on Form 709, the entire contribution is treated as a gift made in 2026 rather than spread over five years. Before making a six-figure contribution, consult a CPA or financial advisor to evaluate how could affect your gift-tax exemption, state tax deduction, and retirement plans.
